items.title: The $0 Part D plan is gone for 2027: stand-alone drug plan premiums are on track to jump 50%, from $34 to $51 a month, for anyone who doesn't switch by Dec 7
items.angle: A usable number with a deadline. KFF says no stand-alone Part D plans will have a $0 premium in 2027, so the 4 million-plus people in one now will pay something unless they shop around. The plan with the lowest average premium nationally is Wellcare Value Script at $6.50. AARP Medicare Rx Preferred goes from $126 to $204.50. The deductible cap rises to $700. The take: compare plans before Dec 7, because staying put is what produces the 50% figure. This pairs with Tuesday's roundup item on the 4.3 million people losing their Advantage or Part D plan.
items.why_now: Open enrollment runs through Dec 7, and KFF published this today (Oct 30). The next Friday roundup still lands with about a month left to switch.
items.is_it_real: This is KFF's independent analysis of CMS 2027 plan data. The $51 average is a projection that assumes current enrollees stay in their plans and leaves out people getting the Low-Income Subsidy. It's an enrollment-weighted average, not anyone's actual bill. KFF puts the jump down mainly to the loss of $0-premium plans. The release doesn't say whether the scaled-back Part D premium stabilization demonstration played a part, so don't claim a cause beyond what KFF says. I checked the numbers against the KFF page today: $34→$51, 4M+ in zero-premium PDPs, Wellcare $6.50, AARP $204.50, $700 deductible cap, $643 average PDP deductible.

items.title: 4.3 million Medicare enrollees will lose their Advantage or Part D plan at year's end, and 1.4 million more are in plans being merged: check your mail before Dec 7
items.angle: A short, useful item for open enrollment: KFF's count from CMS data is 3.1 million Medicare Advantage drug plan enrollees and 1.2 million stand-alone Part D enrollees whose plans end, plus 1.4 million in consolidating plans. It tells readers what a non-renewal notice means and what their options are.
items.why_now: Open enrollment runs through Dec 7, and terminated plans end Dec 31. Pitching is blocked because this is already widely covered, but the number is usable this week.
items.is_it_real: These are KFF's analysis of CMS plan data, an independent source. Before running it, confirm the special enrollment period and Medigap guaranteed-issue rights for people whose plans are not renewed against CMS and Medicare.gov guidance. Don't state them from memory.

items.title: Social Security's 3.6% COLA for 2027 is official: what changes in December checks
items.angle: The Federal Register makes it official: a 3.6% cost-of-living increase effective December 2026, paid in January, plus a 2025 national average wage index of $72,800.33, which moves the taxable maximum and earnings-test limits. One sharp line: how much the Part B premium change takes back.
items.is_it_real: Primary government document. Pair it with the 2027 Part B premium only once CMS publishes that figure; don't estimate it.

items.title: Workers now pay $7,471 a year for family coverage, up 9%, and health costs remain Americans' top money worry
items.angle: KFF's benchmark survey: workers' share of family premiums rose $621 (9%) to $7,471, and people at small firms are hit hardest. KFF polling shows costs are pushing people to delay care. A short item with one usable number, in time for benefits season.
items.why_now: KFF Employer Health Benefits Survey released Oct 22.
items.is_it_real: KFF's independent survey. The digest headline's claim that 'older workers are squeezed hardest' is not in KFF's own summary, which names small-firm workers, so don't use it. That digest item's URL also points to an unrelated KFF SNAP/Medicaid page.
